To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Ca2+ binding in the C- but not N-terminal lobe selectively induces a Ca2+-dependent enhancement of CaV2.l channel open probability, without altering activation or deactivation kinetics, and that the mechanism of facilitation is a relief of basal CaM inhibition in the presence of Ca2+, not a true enhancement.

(a) Ca2+ binding selectively to the C-terminal but not N-terminal lobe induces facilitation of CaV2 (P/Q-type channels), (b) this facilitation represents a true increase in open probability (not simply a relief of inhibition) and (c) this facilitation is due to a slowing of the rate of inactivation (but not activation).

In summary, our research is concerned with
the elementary mechanisms underlying CaM regulation of CaV channels.
the mechanisms of CaV2 channel regulation by calmodulin and the functional implications for Ca2+ channel signaling in the nervous system.
the regulation of the Cav2.1 Ca2+ channel by calmodulin, a process that has been implicated in a wide array of cellular and physiological functions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CaM/CaV2.1 interaction represents an exquisite Ca2+-decoding mechanism with the capacity to sense both local and global Ca2+ signals.
CaM-CaV2.1 interactions are a prime example of the exquisite Ca2+ decoding capacity of CaM.

CaM is the most versatile Ca2+ sensor known to date, with its two lobes each capable of decoding the local/global aspects of Ca2+ signals in a manner that is distinct and selective for the CaV2-1 channels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CDF represents the first example of CaM-triggered facilitation of channel gating.
the local/global CaM selectivity of CaV1.2 and CaV2.2 is recapitulated in the CaV2. 1 channel, and that CDF represents an enhancement of CaV2.1 channel opening.
CaV2. 1 channels are endowed with a unique mechanism for Ca2+-dependent modulation that can be triggered by either Ca2+ influx into, or out of, the channel pore.
The main takeaway from our work is that

Ca2+ ions can be selectively and differentially decoded by CaM to yield distinct forms of regulation of CaV1 channels, which in turn can be selectively and distinctively decoded by the lobes of the same CaM molecule.
the C-terminal lobo of CaM, in concert with the N-terminus of the CaV2. subunits, can generate a novel form of facilitation that is both Ca2+ dependent and local in nature.

the C-terminal lobo of CaM, when attached to CaV2.2 and CaV2.3, triggers a local Ca2+ preference that produces facilitation of channel opening; this mechanism appears to be conserved in CaV2.4 (R-type) channels, and is now shown to also be present in CaV2 channels.
